title: Stones, an Altar and Twelve Curses
sum: The long speech of laws is over, and Moses with the elders gives the people a ceremony to perform once they cross the Jordan. They are to set up great plastered stones on Mount Ebal, write on them all the words of this law, build an altar of uncut stones, and eat peace offerings there in joy. Moses and the Levite priests declare that today Israel has become the people of the LORD.

Then six tribes are to stand on Mount Gerizim to bless and six on Mount Ebal for the curse, while the Levites call out twelve curses. Each targets a wrong that can be done in secret: a hidden idol, contempt for parents, a moved boundary marker, a misled blind man, injustice to the weak, incest, a killing no one sees, a bribe for innocent blood, and at last any failure to make the whole law stand. After each one, all the people answer, "Amen."
readings: Read as a covenant ceremony

The chapter is a rite of entry. Writing the law in public, sacrificing, eating before God, and saying "Amen" to curses were how ancient peoples sealed a treaty. Joshua carries it out at Shechem (Joshua 8:30–35), and the place remained a center of covenant-making (Joshua 24).
Read as a conscience for the community

The twelve curses reach where no judge can see. By saying "Amen," every Israelite agrees that God will judge the secret sins that courts miss. The list protects the people least able to protect themselves: parents, neighbors, the blind, foreigners, orphans and widows.

views.H: Moses commands a ceremony that Joshua performs soon after the crossing (Joshua 8:30–35). Ebal is the place Moses named, and an altar there fits the first sacrifices in the land.
views.C: Most critical scholars see several layers: a stone-and-altar tradition from Shechem (27:1–8), a blessing-and-curse rite on two mountains (27:11–13) and a Levite curse liturgy (27:14–26). Its Shechem setting is surprising in a book that limits sacrifice to one chosen place (chapter 12), which suggests old northern traditions.
views.T: Treaties were written on stone and set up in public, and their curses were sworn by the vassal. The stones and the twelve "Amens" turn the people into a vassal swearing loyalty to the great King.
views.J: The Mishnah describes the ceremony in detail: the ark in the valley, priests and Levites turning to each mountain, and the law written in seventy languages (Mishnah Sotah 7:5). The Talmud counts this as the third covenant, after Horeb and Moab.
views.X: Paul quotes 27:26 in Galatians 3:10 to show that the law brings a curse on those who rely on it, and says that "Christ bought us free from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13).

deep.b: Moses tells Israel to build the altar on Mount Ebal (27:4). The Samaritan Pentateuch reads Mount Gerizim, the Samaritans' holy mountain, and an Old Latin witness agrees. Either Samaritans changed Ebal to Gerizim to support their temple, or Jews changed Gerizim to Ebal to undercut it. The Plain follows the Masoretic "Ebal," backed by Joshua 8:30, but the case for Gerizim is strong: it is the mountain of blessing, a fitting place for an altar and a feast. See the variant on 27:4.

Verses 15 and 24 say "in secret," and the theme runs through the list. Moving a boundary stone at night, misleading a blind man, taking a bribe, or incest inside the household are wrongs that leave no witnesses. Courts need two or three witnesses (19:15). These curses hand such cases to God. The final curse widens it to the whole law (27:26), so that every Israelite takes responsibility for the covenant, not only for the crimes a court can punish.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the altar on the mountain of the curse
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. The altar, the burnt offerings and the peace-offering feast are all placed on Ebal, the mountain where the curse is pronounced (27:4–7, 13), not on Gerizim, the mountain of blessing. If the Masoretic reading is original, the arrangement may be deliberate: the place of sacrifice and joyful eating is set where the curse stands, as if to say that the covenant's curse is met by sacrifice and communion with God. Christian readers may see a pattern here that Paul develops, with the curse taken up at the place of sacrifice (Galatians 3:13). Some Christian commentators have made similar observations. The theory depends on the Ebal reading, which is disputed.

echoes: 11:26–30; Exodus 20:25; Exodus 24:4–8; Joshua 8:30–35; Joshua 24:1–27; Leviticus 18:6–23; Leviticus 19:14; Galatians 3:10–13; John 4:20

settings.what: Stones and an altar on Mount Ebal
settings.by: Moses and the elders of Israel
settings.to: All Israel, to be done on the day they cross the Jordan
settings.when: a ceremony for the first days in the land
settings.why: The people must set up large plastered stones on Mount Ebal and write all the words of this law on them. They must build an altar of uncut stones and eat there with joy. The law is to be public, written in the land itself. Joshua 8:30–35 tells how it was done.
views: The Samaritan Pentateuch and one Old Latin witness read Mount Gerizim in 27:4. The Samaritans built their temple there.

settings.what: Today you have become the LORD's people
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.why: "Today you have become the people of the LORD your God" (27:9). The new generation becomes the covenant people on the plains of Moab, before it enters the land.

settings.what: Twelve curses at Ebal and Gerizim
settings.by: Moses (giving the words the Levites are to call out)
settings.to: All Israel, with six tribes on Mount Gerizim and six on Mount Ebal, in the land
settings.when: to be done after the crossing
settings.why: The Levites call out twelve curses, and all the people answer "Amen." Each one names a wrong done in secret, where no court can reach. Among them are a hidden idol, a moved boundary marker and a misled blind man. Others are injustice to the foreigner, orphan or widow, a hidden killing, and a bribe. The people curse themselves if they do these things. So God becomes the judge of what no one sees.

title: If You Listen, If You Will Not Listen
sum: The great blessings and curses of the covenant. If Israel truly listens to the LORD, it will be blessed in city and field, in children, crops and herds, in coming in and going out. Enemies will flee seven ways, rain will come in its season, and Israel will lend to nations and be the head, not the tail.

If Israel will not listen, every blessing turns into a curse, and the list grows four times as long. Disease, drought, defeat and madness come first, then a foreign nation swooping like an eagle, a siege so terrible that parents eat their children, scattering among the nations, and at last a return to Egypt in ships, as slaves no one will buy. The chapter undoes the exodus step by step, and many readers, Jewish and Christian, have heard their own history in it.
readings: Read as covenant sanctions

Like the treaties of the time, the covenant closes with what happens if it is kept or broken. The closest match in wording is the loyalty oath of Esarhaddon of Assyria (672 BC), which has the bronze sky and iron ground and the eating of children. Moses presents the LORD as the great King whose treaty Israel swears.
Read as prophecy and history

The curses read like an outline of what happened: Assyrian and Babylonian invasions, kings led into exile, sieges and famine, dispersion among the nations, and the flight to Egypt (Jeremiah 43–44). Traditional readers see prophecy; critical readers see a text shaped by those events. Jewish readers have also read it as the story of the long exile after Rome.

views.H: Moses foresees Israel's future: the warnings were given before the land was entered, and the later prophets (Jeremiah, Ezekiel) apply them to their own day.
views.C: Many scholars date the core of the chapter to the 7th century BC, when Judah was a vassal of Assyria, because of its close match with Esarhaddon's oath (28:23, 53). The verses on exile and scattering (28:36–37, 63–68) are often thought to have been added during or after the Babylonian exile.
views.T: This chapter is where the treaty reading is strongest. Kitchen and Kline compare the older Hittite treaties, where curses also follow blessings; Weinfeld and Steymans show that whole sequences of curses match Esarhaddon's text and argue for direct borrowing.
views.J: The section 28:15–68 is the Tokhechah, "the rebuke." In the synagogue it is read quietly and quickly. The Talmud allowed a break between readers here, since Moses spoke these curses on his own (Megillah 31b), but later custom reads them without one. Ramban read it as the second exile, after the Roman destruction.
views.X: Christian readers have heard echoes in Jesus' warnings over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–44; Luke 21:20–24) and in the fall of the city in AD 70. Early Christian writers read the Greek of 28:66, "your life hanging before your eyes," as a picture of Christ on the cross.

deep.b: The curses run Israel's story backward. The diseases of Egypt return (28:27, 60). The people become "a sign and a wonder" (28:46), the phrase used of the plagues. They are scattered instead of gathered, become few instead of as many as the stars (28:62; compare 1:10), and are finally shipped back to Egypt to be sold as slaves (28:68). The blessings, too, echo Genesis: the fruit of the womb and of the soil, enemies fleeing, Israel set over the nations. The covenant gives life; breaking it unmakes Israel.

Does the chapter teach that obedience earns wealth? Within the covenant, blessing and curse describe the life of a whole people in God's land, as a king's treaty promised protection or punishment. Other books push back against a simple rule for individuals: Job, Ecclesiastes and many psalms ask why the righteous suffer, and Jesus denies that disaster proves guilt (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:2–3). Jewish and Christian teachers alike have warned against turning Deuteronomy 28 into a promise of private prosperity.

Verses 52–57 are among the most terrible in Scripture, describing a gentle man and a pampered woman who will hide and eat their own children in a siege. They are not exaggeration: 2 Kings 6:28–29, Lamentations 2:20 and 4:10, and Josephus (Jewish War 6.201–213) record that it happened. The detail is meant to shock a comfortable people into faithfulness.

echoes: Leviticus 26:3–45; Exodus 9:9–11; 2 Kings 6:24–29; 2 Kings 17:6–23; 2 Kings 25:1–21; Jeremiah 5:15–17; Lamentations 2:20; Lamentations 4:10; Amos 4:6–11; Amos 5:11; Hosea 8:13; Luke 21:20–24; Galatians 3:10

settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.when: at the end of the second speech
settings.why: If Israel listens to the LORD, it will be blessed in city and field, children and crops, and set above the nations. If not, every blessing turns into a curse. The curses end in siege, scattering among the nations, and a return to Egypt as slaves no one will buy. The list of curses is four times longer, to make the danger plain. For a people about to enter the land, it puts their whole future in the balance. For readers in Judah and in exile, it named what they saw happen.
views: Ancient treaties ended with blessings and curses. Weinfeld showed that 28:26–35 follows the order of the curses in Esarhaddon's treaty of 672 BC. Steymans argues that 28:20–44 was adapted from one long curse of that treaty. Many date the chapter to the 7th century on that basis.

Others, critical and traditional, think Deuteronomy drew on a common treaty tradition, not on this one text. Carly Crouch doubts direct dependence on Esarhaddon's treaty. Kitchen answers that blessings and curses belong to treaties of every period.
Traditional readers take the chapter as Moses' prophetic warning, fulfilled in 722 BC, in 586 BC, and, for many Jewish readers, in the Roman wars.

title: All of You, Standing Here Today
sum: In the land of Moab Moses gathers all Israel to enter a covenant, "besides the covenant he had made with them at Horeb." He reminds them of the wonders in Egypt and the forty years in the wilderness, when their clothes did not wear out, and says that God has not yet given them a mind to understand. Everyone stands there: leaders and water carriers, women, children and foreigners. The covenant is also made with those "not here with us today," every later generation.

Moses warns of the one person who thinks, "All will be well with me," while secretly serving other gods. Every curse will settle on him. If the nation as a whole turns away, foreigners will see its land burned like Sodom and will ask why, and the answer will be: they abandoned the covenant. The chapter ends with a famous saying: the hidden things belong to the LORD, but what has been revealed belongs to us, to do.
readings: Read as a covenant renewal

A new generation, which did not stand at Sinai as adults, now takes the oath. Ancient kings renewed treaties when a vassal's heir took the throne; Israel renews its covenant on the edge of the land. Joshua 24 and Nehemiah 9–10 show later renewals.
Read as a word to every generation

The words "today" and "not here with us today" make the covenant a present event for each reader. Jews reading this portion before Rosh Hashanah, and Christians reading it as a call to commitment, have heard themselves addressed: you are standing here today.

views.H: The covenant in Moab, forty years after Sinai, renews the Horeb covenant with the generation that will enter the land. Moses speaks of later generations and of exile by prophecy.
views.C: Many critical scholars see 29:22–28 and 30:1–10 as written for exiles: the question "why has the LORD done this?" and the answer "as it is today" sound like reflections after the fall of Jerusalem. The "Moab covenant" may express a theology for those outside the land.
views.T: The chapter has the treaty pattern in small: history (29:2–8), the parties (29:10–15), the stipulation of loyalty (29:16–19), and curses (29:20–28). The question of the nations has a close parallel in the annals of Ashurbanipal.
views.J: The portion Nitzavim (29:10–30:20) is read on the Sabbath before Rosh Hashanah. The Talmud says that the souls of all future Jews and converts stood there (Shevuot 39a). The large letter in 29:28 and the dots over 29:29 drew rabbinic debates about the lost tribes and about communal responsibility.
views.X: Paul quotes 29:4 in Romans 11:8 for Israel's partial hardening, and Hebrews 12:15 warns against "a root of bitterness" from 29:18. Reformed churches have used "those not here today" to include children in the covenant.

deep.b: Verse 29 closes the warning about the secret idolater: God sees and judges what is hidden, and the community acts on what is known. It also became a rule for theology. Jewish teachers have used it to discourage speculation about the end and about the reasons for the commandments; Calvin used it to limit inquiry into predestination. The dots that Hebrew scribes placed over "for us and for our children" show that the verse puzzled readers from very early times.

Few lists in the Torah are as complete as 29:10–11: chiefs, tribes, elders, officers, every man, children, wives, foreigners, woodcutters and water carriers. The covenant is not only for heads of households or the religious elite. The same breadth returns in 31:12 for the seventh-year reading. The rabbis and modern readers both see here the covenant's claim on the whole community, including those on its margins.

echoes: 5:2–3; 8:2–4; Exodus 24:3–8; Joshua 24:1–28; Nehemiah 9:38–10:39; 1 Kings 9:8–9; Jeremiah 22:8–9; Romans 11:8; Hebrews 12:15; Acts 2:39

settings.what: Moses' third speech: the covenant in Moab
settings.to: All Israel in the land of Moab: chiefs, elders and officers, men, women and children, the foreigner in the camp, the woodcutter and water carrier, and those not yet born
settings.when: a covenant made in Moab, "besides the covenant he had made with them at Horeb" (29:1)
settings.why: Moses calls the people to enter the covenant by oath. It is made with everyone present and with every later generation (29:14–15). He warns against the one who secretly thinks he is safe while serving other gods. He foresees a land burned like Sodom. Then he looks past the curses to return, and ends by setting life and death before them. The speech turns the law into a personal choice for each hearer.
views: Traditional readers take it as Moses' last covenant speech.
Many critical scholars date chapters 29–30 to the exile. They speak to people who are outside the land, as Israel in Moab was. They promise that turning back is possible.

settings.what: The oath: all of you, standing here today
settings.to: Everyone in the camp, from leaders to water carriers, the foreigner among them, and those not here today
settings.why: No one stands outside the covenant: leaders and servants, women and children, foreigners, and those not yet born. Moses warns that anyone who blesses himself while turning to other gods will bear every curse. The section ends with a famous line: hidden things belong to the LORD, but what is revealed is for us and our children to do (29:29).

title: Choose Life
sum: Moses looks past the curses to a time when Israel, scattered among the nations, takes the words to heart and returns to the LORD. Then the LORD will turn back their captivity, gather them even from the edge of the sky, bring them into the land, and circumcise their hearts so that they love him with all their heart and being. The curses will move onto their enemies.

The command is not too hard and not far away. No one has to climb into the sky or cross the sea to get it: "the word is very close to you, in your mouth and in your heart." So Moses sets before Israel life and good, death and evil, calls heaven and earth as witnesses, and urges: "Choose life," by loving the LORD, listening to him and holding on to him, for he is your life.
readings: Read as a promise of restoration

Verses 1–10 promise more than a second chance: God himself will change Israel's heart. The prophets develop this into the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Ezekiel 36:24–28). Maimonides read it as a firm promise that Israel will repent and be redeemed.
Read as a call to decision

Verses 11–20 turn to the present: the word is near, the choice is now. This passage shaped Jewish and Christian thinking about free will, from Sirach to Erasmus and Luther, and about the nearness of God's word, from Baruch to Paul.

views.H: Moses predicts the exile and the return, and calls the generation before him to choose faithfulness. The promise of a circumcised heart looks forward to God's future work.
views.C: Critical scholars commonly date 30:1–10 to the exile, because it speaks of scattering and gathering as present facts and uses the language of Jeremiah. 30:11–20 is often read as the original conclusion of the Moab covenant.
views.T: The call to heaven and earth as witnesses (30:19) matches the witness lists of treaties, with creation in place of the gods. The choice between life and death echoes treaty language: loyalty brings life, rebellion brings death.
views.J: The chapter is read in the portion Nitzavim before the Days of Awe, which makes it central to the theme of teshuvah, "return." The rabbis used 30:12, "It is not in the sky," to show that the Torah is interpreted by human sages (Bava Metzia 59b).
views.X: Paul reads 30:12–14 as "the word of faith" about Christ (Romans 10:6–8), and 30:6 as the heart circumcision of the Spirit (Romans 2:29). Christians in many traditions have preached "Choose life" as a call to faith.

deep.b: The Hebrew verb shuv, "turn, return," appears seven times in 30:1–10. Israel will turn the words back to its heart (30:1), turn back to the LORD (30:2, 8, 10); the LORD will turn back its captivity, turn back to gather it (30:3), and turn again to rejoice over it (30:9). Repentance and restoration are two sides of one turning. Jewish tradition took this chapter as the foundation of the laws of teshuvah.

Ancient stories told of heroes who climbed to heaven or crossed the sea to find wisdom or life, like Gilgamesh searching for the plant of life. Moses says Israel needs no such hero. The command has been given; it is in their mouths when they recite it and in their hearts when they take it in. Baruch 3:29–30 applies the words to Wisdom; Paul applies them to Christ, who has come down and risen, so that no one needs to bring him (Romans 10:6–8).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the near word answers the hidden things
deep.b: This is my own reading, though it overlaps with commentators who link the two passages. Deuteronomy 29:29 sets "what is hidden" with God and "what has been made known" with Israel, "so that we will carry out every word of this law." Chapter 30 then contrasts a word that is "in the sky" or "across the sea" with a word that is "very close ... for you to do" (30:11–14). The two passages seem to frame the restoration promise (30:1–10) as one argument: what Israel needs in order to live is not hidden, so its failure cannot be blamed on God's silence. If this is right, "the hidden things" in 29:29 are not mainly a warning against curiosity but a reassurance that the revealed word is enough.

echoes: 4:29–31; 10:16; Leviticus 26:40–45; 1 Kings 8:46–50; Jeremiah 29:10–14; Jeremiah 31:31–34; Ezekiel 36:24–28; Romans 2:29; Romans 10:5–10; Baruch 3:29–30; Sirach 15:15–17

settings.what: When you return, God will return you
settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.when: looking ahead to a time when Israel is scattered among the nations
settings.why: The curses will scatter Israel. But when Israel takes the words to heart and returns to the LORD, God will turn back their captivity. He will gather them, bring them into the land, and circumcise their hearts. The command to circumcise the heart (10:16) becomes God's own work. For exiles, this is the promise that the story is not over. Jeremiah 31:31–34 and Ezekiel 36:24–28 make the same promise.
views: Traditional readers hear Moses foreseeing exile and return.
Critical scholars think it was written in the exile, as hope for those who had already suffered the curses.

settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.when: the end of the third speech
settings.why: The command is not far away, in the sky or across the sea: "The word is close by you, very close: in your mouth and in your heart" (30:14). So Moses calls heaven and earth as witnesses and sets life and death before them. He says: "Choose life" (30:19). The words make every hearer responsible for the choice. Paul applies 30:12–14 to faith in Christ (Romans 10:6–8).

traditions.q: Moses says "choose life" (30:19). Can fallen people choose to turn to God?
views: Yes, with grace. The fall weakened free will but did not destroy it, and the will cooperates with God's grace, which always comes first (Council of Trent, Session 6, canons 4–5). Erasmus, a Catholic, cited this verse against Luther, and Catholic writers also point to Sirach 15:14–17, which is part of the Catholic Old Testament.

Not by their own power. A command shows what we ought to do, not what we can do, and fallen people can do outward good but cannot truly love God without the Holy Spirit (Luther, The Bondage of the Will; Augsburg Confession, article 18).

Fallen people have lost all ability to will any spiritual good that leads to salvation (Westminster Confession 9.3). The call to choose life is answered when God himself circumcises the heart, as 30:6 promises.

Yes. Human beings keep the image of God and their freedom, and salvation is synergy, God's grace and human will working together. The Orthodox have never shared the Western debate's view that the will is in bondage.

Left alone, no. But God's prevenient grace, the grace that goes before, reaches every person and restores the freedom to respond, so all can choose life (Wesley, On Working Out Our Own Salvation; Articles of Religion 8).

title: Moses Hands Over
sum: Moses, now 120, tells Israel he will not cross the Jordan. The LORD will go ahead of them, and Joshua will lead them. Before all Israel he tells Joshua, "Be strong and bold," and promises that the LORD will not let him down or abandon him. Moses writes down "this law," gives it to the priests and elders, and commands that it be read to all the people, men, women, children and foreigners, every seventh year at the Feast of Booths.

At the tent of meeting the LORD appears in the cloud and tells Moses something grim: after his death the people will turn to other gods, and God will hide his face. So Moses is to write a song and teach it, so that it will testify against them when disaster comes. Moses writes the song, finishes writing the law in a scroll, and has the scroll placed beside the ark as a witness. Then he gathers the elders and recites the song.
readings: Read as a handover of leadership

The chapter passes Moses' authority to two successors: Joshua, who leads the people into the land, and the written scroll, read publicly and kept by the priests. Leadership by a person and leadership by a text begin side by side.
Read as a sad farewell

Moses' last days are shadowed by God's prediction that Israel will fail. The song, the scroll and heaven and earth are all set up as witnesses against a people who have not yet sinned. Yet the same chapter twice promises that God will not abandon his people (31:6, 8).

views.H: Moses writes the law, appoints Joshua, and receives the song from God shortly before his death; the chapter records how the Torah began to be preserved and read.
views.C: Critical scholars see several strands: Deuteronomic material about Joshua and the reading of the law (31:1–13, 24–29), an older passage at the tent of meeting (31:14–15, 23), and an introduction to the Song (31:16–22, 30). The written scroll of this law is often linked to the scroll found in Josiah's temple (2 Kings 22).
views.T: Treaties required a copy to be placed in a sanctuary and read publicly at intervals. The scroll beside the ark and the seventh-year reading follow this pattern closely.
views.J: The seventh-year reading is Hakhel, "Gather!" In the Mishnah the king reads Deuteronomy in the temple (Sotah 7:8). From 31:19 the rabbis derived the last commandment in the Torah's order (number 613 in Sefer HaChinukh): every Jew must write a Torah scroll (Sanhedrin 21b).
views.X: Hebrews 13:5 makes the promise of 31:6 God's word to every believer: "I will never let you down, and I will never abandon you." Christians have seen in Joshua (Greek Iesous) a figure of Jesus, who leads God's people into their rest (Hebrews 4:8).

deep.b: This chapter is the Bible's first account of Scripture being written, stored and read. Moses writes the law (31:9, 24), the Levites keep it beside the ark (31:26), and the whole people hear it at fixed times (31:10–13). Nehemiah 8 shows such a reading at the Feast of Booths after the exile, and Josiah reads the found scroll to the people (2 Kings 23:2). The synagogue's weekly reading of the Torah grew from this practice.

Why a song? Laws can be forgotten, but songs stay in the mouth (31:21). When disaster comes, Israel will find that its own song explains what happened: God was faithful, Israel was not. Israel will carry the song into exile, where it will testify, and also hold out hope, since it ends with God's mercy (32:36–43).

echoes: Numbers 27:12–23; Joshua 1:1–9; Joshua 8:34–35; 2 Kings 22:8–13; 2 Kings 23:1–3; Nehemiah 8:1–18; 1 Chronicles 28:20; Hebrews 4:8; Hebrews 13:5

settings.to: All Israel, and then Joshua before them
settings.when: Moses is 120 and will not cross the Jordan
settings.why: Moses tells the people that the LORD and Joshua will go ahead of them. Before them all he tells Joshua, "Be strong and bold" (31:7). The public charge makes Joshua's authority clear to the people, and Joshua 1 picks up the same words.

settings.what: Read the law every seven years
settings.to: The Levite priests who carry the ark and all the elders of Israel; and through them all Israel, men, women, children and the foreigner
settings.when: every seventh year, the year of release, at the Feast of Booths, at the chosen place
settings.why: Moses writes the law and gives it to the priests and elders. It must be read aloud to all the people. Then every generation, even children who did not know it, will hear and learn to fear the LORD. The law answers how the covenant will outlive Moses: by a written book read in public.
views: The Mishnah and Talmud (tractate Sotah) say the king read from Deuteronomy at this ceremony, and tell of King Agrippa doing so.

settings.what: God's charge to Joshua, and a song as witness
settings.to: Moses and Joshua, at the tent of meeting
settings.when: after Moses' charge to Joshua, near Moses' death
settings.why: God warns that after Moses dies the people will turn to other gods, and he will hide his face. So Moses must write a song and teach it, so that it will testify against them when disaster comes. God himself charges Joshua to be strong and bold. The song is meant for a people who have already failed, to explain why trouble has come.

settings.what: Moses gives the book to the Levites
settings.to: The Levites who carry the ark of the covenant, and the elders and officials of the tribes (31:28)
settings.when: when Moses has finished writing the law in a book
settings.why: The book is placed beside the ark as a witness against Israel. Moses knows how rebellious they have been and will be. He gathers the elders and officials to hear the song. The words explain where the written law is kept and why it matters: it will stand when Moses is gone.

title: The Song of Moses
sum: Moses calls heaven and earth to listen. The Song praises God, the Rock, whose work is flawless, and accuses Israel of corruption. When the Most High divided the nations, he kept Jacob for himself, found him in a howling desert, guarded him like the pupil of his eye, carried him like an eagle, and fed him with honey from the rock. But Jeshurun grew fat and kicked, sacrificing to demons and forgetting the God who gave him birth.

So God will hide his face, send famine, plague, beasts and the sword, and make Israel jealous with a "not-people." Yet he stops short of destroying them, lest the enemy boast. Vengeance belongs to him; he will judge for his people when their strength is gone, and ask where their gods are now: "I, only I, am he; I kill and I make alive." The Song ends calling the heavens and the gods to rejoice. Moses tells Israel that this word is their life, and God tells Moses to climb Mount Nebo and die.
readings: Read as a covenant lawsuit
The Song takes the form of a case in court: witnesses called, God's kindness reviewed, Israel accused and sentenced. The prophets often use this pattern (Isaiah 1; Micah 6; Jeremiah 2).
Read as a song of hope

The Song does not end in judgment. Once Israel is helpless, God turns on its enemies and makes atonement for his land. Israel in exile could sing it as both confession and promise, and Paul used it to argue that God has not abandoned Israel (Romans 10–11; Romans 15:10).

views.H: Moses composed the Song at God's command (31:19, 22) as a prophetic witness against the future unfaithfulness of Israel.
views.C: Scholars date the Song anywhere from the 11th century BC (Eissfeldt, Albright, on its archaic language) to the exile. Its picture of God dividing the nations among the "sons of God" (32:8) and calling the gods to bow (32:43, in the scroll) is often seen as an old layer of Israelite religion, which later scribes softened.
views.T: G. Ernest Wright read the Song as a riv, a covenant lawsuit, the poetic form a great king might use to accuse a rebellious vassal. Heaven and earth, the treaty witnesses of 30:19 and 31:28, are summoned in its first line.
views.J: Ha'azinu is read on the Sabbath between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, or just after. The opening of 32:4 begins the burial prayer Tziduk ha-Din. The rabbis found the resurrection in 32:39 and the blessing before Torah study in 32:3.
views.X: The New Testament quotes the Song often: 32:21 in Romans 10:19, 32:35 in Romans 12:19 and Hebrews 10:30, 32:43 in Romans 15:10 and Hebrews 1:6, and 32:17 in 1 Corinthians 10:20. Revelation 15:3 has the victors sing "the song of Moses, the slave of God, and the song of the Lamb."

deep.h: The sons of God and the gods
deep.b: Two of the Song's lines have come down in different forms. At 32:8 the Masoretic Text says God set the borders of the nations "by the number of the sons of Israel," but a Dead Sea Scroll has "sons of God" and the Greek "angels of God." At 32:43 the scroll and the Greek have a line, "all you gods, bow down to him," that the Masoretic lacks. Most textual scholars think the scroll is older in both places, and that scribes removed language that sounded like other gods. The Plain follows the scroll. Read this way, the Song frames itself with the heavenly beings: they receive the nations at the start, and they bow to Israel's God at the end. See the variants on 32:8 and 32:43.

deep.h: God as Rock, father, mother and eagle
deep.b: The Song is rich in pictures of God. He is the Rock, solid and safe (32:4, 15, 18, 30, 31). He is a father who made Israel (32:6) and a mother in labor with him (32:18). He is an eagle stirring its nest and carrying its young (32:11), and a warrior with arrows and a flashing sword (32:23, 41–42). He hides his face (32:20), stores up judgment (32:34) and swears by his own life (32:40). No single image is enough.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two edits, one concern
deep.b: This builds on the work of Tov, Heiser and others, but the connection I draw is my own emphasis. The Masoretic Text differs from the oldest Hebrew evidence at exactly the two points where the Song speaks of heavenly beings: 32:8 ("sons of God" became "sons of Israel") and 32:43 ("all you gods, bow down" is missing). If both changes come from one scribal circle, then the edits were not careless copying but a single theological policy, and the original Song had a deliberate frame: the nations given to the sons of God at the start, those same powers bowing to the LORD at the end. The Song's central claim, "there is no god alongside me" (32:39), would then be a claim about rank and power, not a denial that other heavenly beings exist.

echoes: 31:19–30; Exodus 15:1–18; Psalm 78; Psalm 82; Psalm 90; Isaiah 1:2–4; Isaiah 43:10–13; Micah 6:1–5; Hosea 9:10; Romans 10:19; Romans 12:19; Romans 15:10; 1 Corinthians 10:4; 1 Corinthians 10:20–22; Hebrews 1:6; Hebrews 10:30; Revelation 15:3

settings.to: The whole assembly of Israel (31:30), with the heavens and the earth called as witnesses
settings.when: at the end of Moses' life, to be learned by heart by every generation
settings.why: The Song is a lawsuit in poetry. God, the Rock, is faithful. Israel, fed and carried like an eagle's young, grew fat and turned to other gods. So God hides his face and sends disaster. But he stops short of ending them, lest the enemy boast, and in the end he will judge for his people. It was given to be sung by a people who had suffered for their unfaithfulness. They would see that God was just, and still on their side.
views: Eissfeldt, Albright and Sanders date the Song's language and ideas to the 11th–9th centuries BC, long before the book around it.
Others date it to the 8th–6th centuries BC, when foreign armies ruined Israel and Judah.
Traditional readers take it as Moses' song, as 31:22 says.

settings.to: All Israel on the plains of Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho: the new generation, children of those who left Egypt
settings.why: Moses urges the people to take to heart all his words and command their children to keep them. "For this is not an empty word for you. It is your life" (32:47). The book's message in one line: the law is the way to long life in the land.

God tells Moses to climb Mount Nebo, see the land, and die there, as Aaron died on Mount Hor. The reason is that Moses did not treat God as holy at Meribah. The command explains to Israel why their leader will not cross with them.

title: The Blessing of Moses
sum: Before he dies, Moses the man of God blesses the tribes, as Jacob did his sons (Genesis 49). The poem opens with the LORD coming from Sinai, Seir and Paran with ten thousands of holy ones, giving a law, and becoming king in Jeshurun.

Then each tribe is blessed: Reuben may live though few; Judah is helped against his foes; Levi receives the Urim and Thummim and the duty to teach and offer sacrifice; Benjamin rests secure near God; Joseph's land is rich with dew, deep springs, sun and hills, and his horns are a wild ox's; Zebulun and Issachar draw wealth from the sea; Gad is a lion; Dan a lion's cub; Naphtali full of favor; Asher dips his foot in oil. The poem closes in praise: no one is like God, who is Jeshurun's help, whose everlasting arms are beneath, and no people is as happy as Israel, saved by the LORD. Simeon is not mentioned.
readings: Read as a dying father's blessing
Moses acts as the father of the nation, as Isaac and Jacob blessed their sons. The blessings look ahead to the tribes' lands and roles in Canaan.
Read as an ancient hymn

The opening and closing verses (33:2–5, 26–29) form a hymn to God the divine warrior and king, with old poetic language, set around the tribal sayings. Many scholars think it is among the oldest poetry in the Bible.

views.H: Moses pronounces the blessing just before his death. Its prophecies of the tribes' lands, Levi's priesthood and Benjamin's sanctuary were fulfilled after the conquest.
views.C: Frank Moore Cross and David Noel Freedman dated the poem to the 11th or 10th century BC from its archaic Hebrew. Details such as Simeon's absence, Judah's separation (33:7) and Dan's link to Bashan (33:22) suggest a time when the tribes had settled and changed. The verse "Moses commanded us a law" (33:4) speaks of Moses in the third person.
views.T: The blessings show the King's gifts to his loyal people, as treaties promised protection and land to a faithful vassal. The frame celebrates the LORD as king (33:5), the overlord of the covenant.
views.J: The blessing is read on Simchat Torah, the day the yearly Torah reading ends and begins again. Children learn 33:4 as their first verse (Sukkah 42a), and 33:5 is among the kingship verses of Rosh Hashanah.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in the coming of God with holy ones (33:2) a pattern for the second coming (Jude 14–15, quoting 1 Enoch). Hymns such as "Leaning on the Everlasting Arms" drew on 33:27, and many Christians read the final beatitude (33:29) beside Jesus' Beatitudes.

deep.b: Jacob's blessing (Genesis 49) and Moses' (Deuteronomy 33) make an instructive pair. Jacob curses Simeon and Levi for their violence at Shechem (Genesis 34; 49:5–7); Moses praises Levi for its zeal at the golden calf and leaves Simeon out. Jacob gives Judah the scepter; Moses offers a short prayer for Judah. Both give Joseph the longest and richest blessing. Both call one tribe a lion's cub (Judah in Genesis 49:9, Dan in Deuteronomy 33:22). The changes reflect the tribes' different fortunes over time.

Simeon is not named. Its territory lay inside Judah's (Joshua 19:1–9), and it seems to have been absorbed into Judah early. Some Greek manuscripts add Simeon to Reuben's line in 33:6. With Ephraim and Manasseh counted inside Joseph, the list has eleven tribes; readers who want twelve count Joseph's two sons separately.

echoes: Genesis 27:27–29; Genesis 49:1–28; Judges 5:4–5; Habakkuk 3:3–6; Psalm 68:7–17; Exodus 32:26–29; Numbers 23:9; Malachi 2:4–7; Jude 14–15; Matthew 5:3–11

settings.to: The tribes of Israel, each by name
settings.why: Like Jacob in Genesis 49, Moses blesses the tribes before he dies. The poem begins with the LORD coming from Sinai to be king in Jeshurun. It ends with Israel's happiness, "a people saved by the LORD" (33:29). Levi is charged to teach the law and offer sacrifice. The blessing sends the tribes into the land with a word of hope after the warnings of the Song. Simeon is missing, perhaps because it was already absorbed into Judah.
views: Many scholars date the poem, or its tribal sayings, to the time of the judges or the early kings, much earlier than the rest of the book.

title: Moses Dies on Mount Nebo
sum: Moses climbs Mount Nebo, and the LORD shows him the whole land promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: "I have let your eyes see it, but you will not cross over into it." Moses, the servant of the LORD, dies there in Moab at the LORD's word, 120 years old, his eyes still sharp. God himself buries him, and no one knows his grave. Israel mourns thirty days.

Joshua, on whom Moses had laid his hands, is filled with a spirit of wisdom, and the people listen to him. The Torah closes with an epitaph: no prophet has arisen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face, unmatched in the signs and wonders he did in Egypt and before the eyes of all Israel.
readings: Read as an ending

The five books of Moses end outside the promised land, with the promise still ahead. The people must go on with a new leader and a written law. For readers in exile, or anyone waiting on God's promises, the ending is honest about waiting.
Read as a portrait of Moses
The chapter praises Moses above all prophets, yet keeps him human: he dies, he does not enter, his grave is lost. The Bible honors him without allowing his tomb to become a shrine.

views.H: Tradition holds that Joshua wrote the last verses (Bava Batra 15a), or that Moses wrote them in tears at God's dictation (Menachot 30a). The chapter records the end of the Mosaic age.
views.C: "To this day" (34:6) and "no prophet has risen again" (34:10) look back from a later time. Many scholars think the chapter was written to close the Pentateuch as a whole, setting Moses' Torah above all later prophecy, perhaps in the Persian period.
views.T: With the overlord's representative gone, the covenant continues through the appointed successor and the written document, as treaties passed to a vassal's heir.
views.J: The Torah reading ends here on Simchat Torah and begins at once again with Genesis 1. The rabbis taught that Moses died by God's kiss (34:5) and that God buried him, setting the example of burying the dead (Sotah 14a). Maimonides made Moses' unequaled prophecy a principle of faith.
views.X: The New Testament presents Jesus as the prophet like Moses (Acts 3:22–23), greater than Moses as a son is greater than a servant (Hebrews 3:1–6). Moses finally stands in the land with Jesus at the transfiguration (Matthew 17:3), and Jude 9 knows a tradition about the archangel Michael and Moses' body.

deep.b: The Hebrew "he buried him" names no one, so the natural subject is God. The Greek smooths it to "they buried him." Jewish tradition drew from God's act the duty of burying the dead. Later writings imagined more: the Assumption of Moses, which Jude 9 seems to know, told of Michael and the devil disputing over his body; Josephus says Moses vanished in a cloud and wrote of his own death so that no one would say he had been taken up to God. The unknown grave kept anyone from turning it into a place of worship.

deep.title: Claude's theory: an ending for exiles
deep.b: This builds directly on James A. Sanders' Torah and Canon (1972), which argued that the Torah was closed at Moses' death, before the conquest, so that a people in exile could see themselves in it. My addition is to notice how many details in chapters 29–34 fit that audience: a covenant made outside the land (29:1), with those "not here with us today" (29:15), a promise of gathering from the ends of the sky (30:4), a law that is near enough to keep anywhere (30:14), a scroll that travels with the people (31:26), and a leader who sees the land but dies outside it (34:4). The ending turns Moses' story into the story of every generation that has the word but not yet the land.

echoes: 3:23–28; 32:48–52; Numbers 20:22–29; Numbers 27:12–23; Exodus 33:11; Numbers 12:6–8; Joshua 1:1–9; Matthew 17:1–8; Acts 3:22–23; Hebrews 3:1–6; Hebrews 11:13–16; Jude 9

settings.what: The LORD shows Moses the land
settings.why: God shows Moses the whole land sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Moses may see it but not enter. The last words to Moses tie the end of the Torah to the promise of Genesis 12:7. The book closes with Israel still outside the land, waiting. On the critical view, so were the exiles who first read it.
